chunks: Servo advantages over other motors. The question: What are its advantages compared to other types of motors?
A servo's big advantage is that it measures where it is.
Because of that, it reaches its target under any load, it pushes back when disturbed, and it knows when it has failed to arrive.
A stepper only counts steps and trusts that it got there. A plain motor has no idea where it is. The price of the servo's advantage is cost, extra parts, and tuning.
Imagine walking across a dark room by counting exactly 20 paces. That is a stepper. If you slip once, you never find out, and you end up in the wrong spot.
A servo is the same walk with the lights on: you look, see you are short, and take another step. The analogy breaks in one place: the lights cost money.
The sensor, the drive and the tuning all add expense, so for easy jobs counting paces is fine.
Shapes, not data for any specific motor.
The stepper's torque has halved by about 1200 rpm in this model; the servo stays flat until it reaches rated speed, with a dashed peak envelope for short bursts.
The brushed DC at fixed voltage falls linearly from stall torque to no-load speed because back-EMF eats the voltage.
Open loop / closed loop: running without feedback, or with a measured result fed back to correct it. Following error: the gap between commanded and actual position.
A big one raises a fault. Stepper: a motor that moves a fixed step per pulse and never checks where it ended up. Phase (winding): one of a motor's coils of wire.
Current through it makes heat.
Compare two motors sitting still, holding a position. A stepper with 1. 5 amps in each of two phases, 2 ohms each, burns 2 times 1.
5 squared times 2 equals 9 watts in its windings, even with no load. A servo holding a balanced load draws almost nothing, because its current follows the load.
Now overload both: the stepper silently loses steps, and the servo shows a following-error fault.
That is the whole idea: feedback buys accuracy, fault detection and efficient current use.
"A servo's advantage is feedback: it knows where it is, so it's accurate under any load, holds position by pushing back and reports when it fails to arrive.
Its torque stays flat out to rated speed with brief higher peaks, whereas a stepper's torque falls with speed.
It's efficient because current follows load, while a stepper burns full current at rest.
Disadvantages are cost, complexity and tuning, so I'd pick a stepper for simple light low-speed jobs."
